name: Frank Smith

views.text: A struggling run game is a collective problem, never one back's or one lineman's fault.
A smaller back can still win short yardage if he has the feel and timing to find space.
The rookie year is the hardest; the jump comes once the volume of the offense slows down for him.
A disappointing season is something to study, not something to bury.
Consistency comes from daily habits in the spring, not from promises in the summer.
Game plans are built together by the head coach, the coordinator and the position coaches.

signatures: credits the position coaches by name for a player's growth
declines to rank or single out a player when asked to compare him with others
frames problems as execution against the looks the defense showed
want: to be seen as the architect of a lasting run game in his own right, not only as the head coach's partner
fear: that the offense's dips get pinned on him while its best days are credited to the play-caller
voice: Earnest, measured and process-focused; he speaks in long, qualified sentences and avoids blaming individuals. He spreads credit to position coaches and players and turns setbacks into lessons to study. He has a light, self-deprecating humor but rarely makes promises. Public coverage of him is thin, so his voice rests mostly on press-conference transcripts.

evidence.summary: Hiring report: came from the Chargers as run game coordinator and offensive line coach, after tight ends jobs with the Raiders and Bears and an assistant line job with the Saints; the Chargers' run- and pass-block win rates improved under him. Career facts only.

Full transcript: measured and upbeat, he credits position coaches Studesville and Barry, praises players' work habits, declines to rank a tackle, explains receivers' quiet games as collective issues and describes the game plan as a joint process with McDaniel. Primary source; one session.

He explains how the staff decides whether a short-yardage problem needs correction or a scheme change, rejects the idea that Achane is too small for short yardage, and calls run-game efficiency a collective effort. His own explanation, filtered by a beat writer.

Spring 2025: he calls 2024 a letdown with some bright spots, wants the consistency and discipline of 2023 back, and uses the offseason to align players' understanding. The writer describes him as earnest, qualified and process-minded.

evidence.publisher: Pro Football Talk (NBC Sports), Josh Alper
evidence.summary: He says Achane has handled a much bigger 2024 workload professionally and that a rookie season is usually the hardest adjustment. Short news item; shows how he talks up a young player, little else.
